351.title: Laughter (Genesis 21:1–7)
351.hook: Sarah laughs at ninety and names her son Isaac, he laughs
351.howItsDone: Catholics remember Sarah and Abraham as parents in faith, and the Church reads the promise of Isaac alongside the announcement to Mary, where the angel says nothing is impossible with God.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Abraham bargains: fifty, forty, thirty, ten, and God never said no. Your line was argue for mercy. Who did you stand up for? A new week starts with a baby. Day three hundred fifty-one.

A maternity ward. A woman in the bed with white hair. A husband in the chair beside her, a hundred years old, holding a newborn. A nurse walks in, stops, and checks the chart twice. That's the scene in Genesis twenty-one, and the Bible knows exactly how funny it is. Long after the call to go forth, after the stars, after the visitors at the tent, the promise finally arrives. And the whole story of it, from the first announcement to the birth, is threaded with one sound. Not weeping. Not singing. Laughing.
screen: `WHITE HAIR IN THE MATERNITY WARD.` → `A HUNDRED-YEAR-OLD FATHER.` → `ONE SOUND THROUGH IT ALL.`

segments.voice: First, the laughs before. When God first tells Abraham, in chapter seventeen, that Sarah will bear a son, Abraham falls on his face and laughs. A hundred years old, and Sarah ninety? Then at Mamre, when the visitor promises a son by next year, Sarah, listening behind the tent door, laughs to herself. Old and worn out, she thinks, and pleasure now? And the visitor asks, in the Douay-Rheims: "Is there any thing hard to God?" Sarah, embarrassed, says she didn't laugh. And he says: yes, you did. Second, the birth. The Lord visits Sarah as he promised, and she bears a son in her old age, at the very time God said. Third, the name. Abraham calls him Isaac. In Hebrew, Yitzchak: he laughs. The doubting laugh is turned into a name. And Sarah, holding the baby, says this, in the Douay-Rheims: "God hath made a laughter for me: whosoever shall hear of it will laugh with me." The laugh has changed. It started as a snort at the impossible. It ends as joy so big she expects the neighbors to catch it. Fourth, the echo. The visitor's question comes back in the Gospel of Luke. When the angel Gabriel tells Mary she'll bear a son, he points to her elderly cousin Elizabeth, pregnant at last, and says that nothing is impossible with God. Old Sarah and young Mary, two births that make no sense, and the same question underneath: is anything too hard for God?
screen: `ABRAHAM LAUGHS FIRST.` · `SARAH LAUGHS BEHIND THE DOOR.` · `YITZCHAK: HE LAUGHS.` · `NOTHING IMPOSSIBLE, AGAIN IN LUKE.` · then, large: `GOD HATH MADE A LAUGHTER FOR ME.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: laugh at one of God's surprises. Settle, and breathe. Look back over your life for something you were sure would never happen, and then did. A friendship that came out of nowhere. A recovery nobody expected. A child, a job, a phone call, a second chance. Something that made you shake your head. Let yourself smile at it. If a real laugh comes, let it. If you pray, you can give thanks for the surprise that still makes you laugh. The bell holds the time.
Laughter. The sound that runs through the birth of Isaac, whose name means he laughs. It starts as doubt and ends as joy.
Your line: god made me laugh. Today, tell one person the story of a surprise that still makes you laugh, and let them laugh with you. Day three hundred fifty-one.

fork.reveal: "God hath made a laughter for me: whosoever shall hear of it will laugh with me." the snort of doubt has become joy she expects to share.

what it means: a promise that made both parents laugh in disbelief arrives, and the laugh turns into joy.

352.title: God will provide (Genesis 22:1–19)
352.hook: the binding of Isaac, a hard story the Church reads as a figure of the Father's gift
352.carry: the two of them went on together
352.howItsDone: Genesis 22 is one of the Old Testament readings at the Easter Vigil and is read on the Second Sunday of Lent in one year of the cycle; Jews read it at Rosh Hashanah and call it the Akedah.

segments.voice: Yesterday, laughter: Isaac, he laughs, and an old mother who couldn't stop. Your line was god made me laugh. Who did you tell your surprise to? Today, the same boy, and the hardest story in Genesis. Day three hundred fifty-two.

Some stories you can't tidy up, and this is one of them. Jews call it the Akedah, the binding. Christians have painted it for centuries: an old man with a knife raised, a boy on a pile of wood, an angel grabbing the old man's wrist. People who love the Bible still argue about this chapter, and many find it disturbing. That's an honest place to start. The Church doesn't ask anyone to find it easy. It reads it on the holiest night of the year anyway, at the Easter Vigil, because it hears something in it worth the difficulty.
screen: `THE AKEDAH: THE BINDING.` → `A KNIFE, A BOY, AN ANGEL.` → `READ AT THE EASTER VIGIL.`

segments.voice: First, the command. God tests Abraham. In the Douay-Rheims: "Take thy only begotten son Isaac, whom thou lovest." Every phrase tightens the knot: your son, your only one, the one you love, the laughing child of the promise. Go to a mountain in the land of Moria, and offer him there. The text gives no word of Abraham's feelings. He rises early, saddles the donkey, splits the wood. Silence. Second, the walk. Three days. Then Abraham puts the wood on Isaac's back, and takes the fire and the knife in his own hands, and the two of them go on together. Isaac speaks once: father, here is the fire and the wood, but where is the victim? And Abraham answers, in the Douay-Rheims: "God will provide himself a victim for an holocaust, my son." And again: the two of them went on together. Third, the stopping. At the top, Abraham builds the altar, binds Isaac, and raises the knife, and the angel of the Lord calls his name twice. Don't lay your hand on the boy. Abraham looks up and sees a ram caught by its horns in a thicket. He names the place: the Lord sees, or the Lord will provide. Fourth, how the Church reads it. The Letter to the Hebrews says Abraham reckoned God could raise the dead. The Church Fathers saw Christ in Isaac carrying his own wood up a hill, and in the ram given in his place. The Catechism reads it as a figure of the Father who does not spare his own Son. Abraham's son was spared. The Church hears the Father's Son was not.
screen: `THY ONLY BEGOTTEN, WHOM THOU LOVEST.` · `THE WOOD ON ISAAC'S BACK.` · `A RAM CAUGHT IN A THICKET.` · `A FIGURE OF THE FATHER'S GIFT.` · then, large: `GOD WILL PROVIDE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: sit with a story you don't fully understand. Today's is a good one to start with. Settle, and breathe. Don't try to solve it. Just let one image stay: a father and son walking up a hill, side by side, the boy carrying the wood. The two of them went on together. Let the questions come, and don't chase them away. Some stories are meant to be carried a long time before they open. If you pray, you can bring your questions to God as they are. The bell holds the time.
Akedah. The binding, the Hebrew name for Abraham's walk up the mountain with Isaac, and the test that ends with a ram and a promise that God will provide. Today's word.
Your line: the two of them went on together. Today, when you hit a need you can't meet yet, say the line and take the next small step anyway. Day three hundred fifty-two.

what it means: a hard story the Church doesn't tidy up, where God stops the knife and provides; Christians hear in it the Father who gives his Son.
what a scholar hears: the Akedah; yir'eh, will see or provide; the Fathers read Isaac with the wood as a type of Christ with the cross.

353.title: Rebecca at the well (Genesis 24)
353.hook: a servant prays for a sign and a young woman waters ten camels
353.howItsDone: Catholics remember Rebecca among the matriarchs of faith, and Genesis 24 is one of the Old Testament readings the Church offers for weddings.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Akedah: a father and son walking up a hill, and a ram in a thicket. Yesterday's line was the two of them went on together. Did it help with a need you couldn't meet yet? Today Isaac is grown, and someone goes looking for his wife. Day three hundred fifty-three.
screen: `THE TWO OF THEM WENT ON TOGETHER.`

segments.voice: Genesis twenty-four is a long chapter, and its hero doesn't even get a name. He's the elder servant of Abraham's house, the one in charge of everything. Abraham, very old now, sends him back to the old country in Mesopotamia to find a wife for Isaac among his own relatives. The servant loads ten camels with gifts and makes the long trip. He arrives at evening, at a well outside the city, at the hour the women come out to draw water. And he has no idea what he's looking for. So he does the only thing he can think of. He prays.
screen: `A SERVANT WITH NO NAME.` → `SENT BACK TO THE OLD COUNTRY.` → `TEN CAMELS AT A WELL.`

segments.voice: First, the prayer. He asks God to show kindness to his master, and he names a sign. Let the young woman to whom I say, let down thy pitcher that I may drink, be the one who answers: drink, and I'll give thy camels drink also. Notice what he's asking for. Not beauty, not wealth. A generous heart. Second, the answer. Before he's even finished praying, Rebecca comes out with a pitcher on her shoulder. He runs to her and asks for a little water. She lowers the jar and gives it to him. And then, in the Douay-Rheims: "And when he had drunk, she said: I will draw water for thy camels also, till they all drink." Third, the size of that offer. Ten camels after a desert journey. She runs back and forth to the well, emptying her jar into the trough, again and again, until every one is done. Nobody asked her to. That's the sign: not that she gave water, but that she did more than she was asked. The servant stands there and watches in silence, wondering. Fourth, the choice. When the family discusses it, they end by asking her. Will you go with this man? And Rebecca says, in the Douay-Rheims: "I will go." Just that. Another person leaving home for a land she hasn't seen, like Abraham before her. The servant bows to the ground and thanks God, whose kindness, he says, has led him the whole way.
screen: `HE PRAYS FOR A GENEROUS HEART.` · `SHE COMES BEFORE HE FINISHES.` · `TEN THIRSTY CAMELS.` · `THEY ASK HER: WILL YOU GO?` · then, large: `THY CAMELS ALSO.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: do more than you're asked. Settle, and breathe. Think of one request you know is coming in the next day. A coworker needs a file. A kid needs help with homework. Your partner asks you to pick up milk. Now picture Rebecca at the trough, jar after jar. What's the camels-too version of that request? Sending the file and offering to look it over. Picking up the milk and the thing they forgot. Choose one. If you pray, you can ask for a generous heart like hers. The bell holds the time.
Chesed, kindness, faithful love: what the servant prayed for, and what Rebecca showed when she watered all ten of his camels. Today's word.
Your line: the camels too. Today, when someone asks you for one thing, give it, and then quietly do the next thing they'll need. Day three hundred fifty-three.

what it means: a servant prays for a generous heart, and a young woman shows it by doing far more than she's asked, then chooses to go.
what a scholar hears: chesed, faithful kindness, runs through the chapter from the servant's prayer to his thanks.

354.title: A bowl of stew (Genesis 25:19–34)
354.hook: Esau sells his birthright because he's hungry right now
354.carry: not for a bowl of stew
354.howItsDone: Catholic tradition speaks of temperance, the virtue of moderating desires, and many Catholics practice small acts of self-denial, especially on Fridays and during Lent.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Rebecca at the well, chesed: ten thirsty camels and a girl who did more than she was asked. Your line was the camels too. What extra did you do? Today, Rebecca's sons. Day three hundred fifty-four.

You walk in starving after a long day. Someone's cooking, and the whole kitchen smells like onions and something slow-simmered. You'd say almost anything for a bowl. Almost anything. Genesis has a story about exactly that moment. The Douay-Rheims calls the dish red pottage, and the Letter to the Hebrews calls it one mess: a single bowl of stew. And the thing sold for it was a firstborn son's whole future.
screen: `STARVING, AND SOMETHING SMELLS GOOD.` → `A MESS OF POTTAGE.` → `SOLD FOR A BOWL OF STEW.`

segments.voice: First, the twins. Rebecca, like Sarah before her, waits years for a child, and Isaac prays for her. When she conceives, the twins struggle so hard inside her that she asks God why. And God tells her: two nations are in your womb, and the elder will serve the younger. Esau is born first, red and hairy. Jacob comes out holding his brother's heel. Esau grows into a hunter, a man of the open field. Jacob is a quiet man who stays among the tents. Isaac favors Esau; Rebecca favors Jacob. You can feel the trouble coming. Second, the stew. One day Jacob is cooking lentils, and Esau comes in from the field, exhausted. Give me some of that red stuff, he says. Jacob, quick as a trader, answers: sell me your birthright first. Third, the birthright. Later, the law in Deuteronomy gives the firstborn son a double share of all his father has. It was a future: the inheritance, and the family's name after the father. And Esau says, I'm about to die, what good is a birthright to me? He swears it away, eats, drinks, gets up, and leaves. Fourth, the verdict. Genesis doesn't lecture. It just ends the scene with one line. In the Douay-Rheims, Esau went his way, "making little account of having sold his first birthright." The Letter to the Hebrews later remembers him as the man who traded his birthright for a single meal. Neither brother looks good here. Jacob drives a hard bargain with a hungry man. But the story's eye is on what Esau threw away for right now.
screen: `TWINS STRUGGLING IN THE WOMB.` · `GIVE ME THAT RED STUFF.` · `A DOUBLE SHARE AND A FUTURE.` · `MAKING LITTLE ACCOUNT OF IT.` · then, large: `NOT FOR A BOWL OF STEW.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: delay one small want. Settle, and breathe. Notice what you're craving right now, or what you usually reach for at this hour. A snack, a scroll, a coffee, a quick look at your messages. Don't fight it. Just name it, and decide to wait until the bell rings. Notice the pull of right now, the Esau pull. Then notice whether you're still fine without it. If you pray, you can offer the waiting for something that matters more. The bell holds the time.
Birthright. The firstborn's double share and his place in the family's future. Esau sold his for a bowl of red lentil stew.
Your line: not for a bowl of stew. Today, when something you value is about to be traded for comfort right now, say the line and wait ten minutes. Day three hundred fifty-four.

355.title: The stolen blessing (Genesis 27)
355.hook: Jacob in goatskins deceives his blind father, and Esau weeps
355.howItsDone: Catholics examine their consciences before confession, and the Church teaches that lying offends against truth and that repairing harm done by a lie is part of making amends.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the birthright: Esau traded his future for a bowl of red stew. Your line was not for a bowl of stew. What did you wait ten minutes for? Today, the same brothers, years later. Day three hundred fifty-five.

If you were inventing a holy book to make your people look good, you would not write this chapter. The man the whole nation will be named after, the grandson of Abraham, puts on his brother's clothes, ties goatskins to his arms so he'll feel hairy, carries in a dish his mother cooked, and lies to his blind, aging father's face, more than once. And it works. Genesis tells it in slow, painful detail, as if it wants you to sit in the room. Isaac is old. His eyes have failed. And he wants to bless his favorite son before he dies.
screen: `NOT HOW YOU'D WRITE YOUR HEROES.` → `GOATSKINS AND A BROTHER'S CLOTHES.` → `A BLIND FATHER, AND A LIE.`

segments.voice: First, the plan. Isaac sends Esau out to hunt game and make him the savory meat he loves, so he can bless him. Rebecca overhears. She calls Jacob, has him bring two young goats, cooks them the way Isaac likes, dresses Jacob in Esau's best clothes, and covers his hands and neck with the skins. Jacob worries about being caught, and she says, upon me be thy curse, my son. Second, the scene. Jacob goes in. Isaac is suspicious. You came back so fast? Come close, let me feel you. And then the famous line, in the Douay-Rheims: "The voice indeed is the voice of Jacob; but the hands are the hands of Esau." He asks straight out, are you my son Esau? And Jacob says, I am. Isaac smells the field on his clothes, and blesses him with dew of heaven and fatness of the earth. Third, the other door. Jacob has barely left when Esau comes in with his dish. Who are you? Your firstborn, Esau. And Isaac trembles. Esau roars out with a great cry: "Bless me also, my father." Have you only one blessing, father? And he weeps. A grown man, a hunter, weeping for his father's blessing. Fourth, what the Bible does with it. It doesn't hide it. Augustine read the trick as a mystery pointing beyond itself. Other readers simply let it stand: God's promise goes on through a family that lies, plays favorites and breaks. Esau says in his heart he'll kill his brother. Rebecca sends Jacob away for a few days, she says. Genesis never records her seeing him again.
screen: `A MOTHER'S PLAN, TWO YOUNG GOATS.` · `THE VOICE OF JACOB, THE HANDS OF ESAU.` · `ESAU'S GREAT CRY.` · `THE PROMISE GOES THROUGH A BROKEN HOME.` · then, large: `BLESS ME ALSO, MY FATHER.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: repair one old deception. Settle, and breathe. Let your memory go back, gently, to a time you let someone believe something that wasn't true. Small or not so small. A borrowed thing you said you'd returned. A version of events that made you look better. A credit you didn't correct. Don't punish yourself. Just look at it the way Genesis does: plainly. Then ask what one honest step would look like now. A message, an admission, a correction. If you pray, you can bring it to God first. The bell holds the time.
Berakhah, blessing, in Hebrew: what Jacob stole from his blind father in his brother's clothes, while Esau wept too late. Today's word.
Your line: the bible doesn't hide it. Today, take the honest step you pictured, even a small one, and don't dress it up. Day three hundred fifty-five.

356.title: The ladder (Genesis 28:10–22)
356.hook: a runaway sleeps on a stone and wakes saying the Lord is in this place, and I knew it not
356.howItsDone: The traditional entrance chant for the dedication of a church, Terribilis est locus iste, takes Jacob's words at Bethel, and Genesis 28:11–18 is among the readings the Church offers for that rite.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the stolen blessing, berakhah: goatskins, a blind father, and Esau's bitter cry. Your line was the bible doesn't hide it. Did you take your honest step? Today, the liar is on the run. Day three hundred fifty-six.

Jacob has the blessing. He also has a brother who wants him dead. So he leaves home with almost nothing, walking toward Haran, his uncle's country, alone. By sunset he's somewhere in the hills, nowhere in particular, no inn, no friend, no tent. He picks up a stone, puts it under his head, and lies down on the ground. A night far from home, in a bus station or a hospital chair or a strange city, after something you did went badly wrong: that's this night. It's the last place anyone expects to meet God.
screen: `THE BLESSING, AND A BROTHER'S RAGE.` → `ALONE IN THE HILLS AT SUNSET.` → `A STONE FOR A PILLOW.`

segments.voice: First, the dream. A ladder, or a stairway, stands on the earth, its top reaching heaven, and the angels of God are going up and down on it. Going up first, then down, as if they were already here. And the Lord stands above it. Second, the promise. God doesn't scold Jacob for the lie. God repeats the promise to Abraham: the land, descendants like the dust of the earth, and in you all the families of the earth will be blessed. And then something new, just for him: I will keep you wherever you go, and I will not leave you. Third, the waking. In the Douay-Rheims: "And when Jacob awaked out of sleep, he said: Indeed the Lord is in this place, and I knew it not." And then, trembling: "this is no other but the house of God, and the gate of heaven." He sets up the stone as a pillar, pours oil on it, and calls the place Bethel, which in Hebrew means house of God. A nowhere place in the hills, renamed. Fourth, where the Church hears it. In the Gospel of John, Jesus tells Nathanael he'll see heaven opened and the angels of God ascending and descending upon the Son of man. Christian tradition reads Christ as the ladder itself, the meeting of heaven and earth. And in the Church's traditional chant for the dedication of a church, the Mass opens with Jacob's words in Latin: Terribilis est locus iste, how awesome is this place. A building, consecrated with the words of a runaway who slept on a rock.
screen: `ANGELS GOING UP, THEN DOWN.` · `I WILL NOT LEAVE YOU.` · `BETHEL: HOUSE OF GOD.` · `CHRIST AS THE LADDER.` · then, large: `AND I KNEW IT NOT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: name where God was unnoticed. Settle, and breathe. Think back over the past week. Look for a place or a moment you passed through without a thought: a bus ride, a hard conversation, a waiting room, a sink full of dishes, a sleepless hour. Pick one. Now replay it slowly, as if it were Bethel. What was there that you missed? A kindness, a quiet, a person, a gift. If you pray, you can say Jacob's words about it: the Lord was in this place. If not, simply notice what was there. The bell holds the time.
The ladder. Jacob's dream at Bethel: a stairway between earth and heaven, angels on it, God above, and a promise: I will not leave you.
Your line: and I knew it not. Today, in one ordinary place, a kitchen, a car, a hallway, stop for three breaths and look again. Day three hundred fifty-six.

357.title: Rachel and Leah (Genesis 29)
357.hook: Jacob works seven years for love and is tricked by his uncle
357.howItsDone: Catholics remember Rachel and Leah among the mothers of Israel; the Church's traditional wedding blessing once asked that the bride be loving like Rachel, and Leah's son Judah is named in Jesus's genealogy read at Christmas.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the ladder: a runaway on a stone pillow, and a nowhere place renamed the house of God. Your line was and I knew it not. Where did you look again? Day three hundred fifty-seven, the end of the week.

Jacob arrives in his uncle Laban's country at a well, of course, because in Genesis the important meetings happen at wells. A shepherd girl comes with her father's flock. Her name is Rachel. Jacob rolls the heavy stone off the well's mouth by himself, waters her sheep, kisses her, and bursts into tears. Love at first sight, at a well, in the middle of the day. And the man who tricked his blind father is about to meet someone even better at tricks than he is.
screen: `ANOTHER MEETING AT A WELL.` → `JACOB ROLLS THE STONE AWAY.` → `A TRICKSTER MEETS HIS MATCH.`

segments.voice: First, the bargain. Laban has two daughters: Leah, the elder, whose eyes the text calls weak or tender, and Rachel, the younger, beautiful. Jacob offers seven years of work for Rachel. And then one of the loveliest lines in Genesis, in the Douay-Rheims: "So Jacob served seven years for Rachel: and they seemed but a few days, because of the greatness of his love." Second, the trick. On the wedding night, Laban sends in Leah, veiled, in the dark. In the morning, Jacob finds Leah. Why hast thou deceived me? he asks. And Laban answers that in their country, the younger isn't given before the firstborn. The man who disguised himself as the firstborn has been fooled by a firstborn in disguise. Genesis doesn't point it out. It doesn't need to. Jacob works seven more years for Rachel. Third, the one nobody chose. Leah is married to a man who loves her sister. And here the text turns its eye to her: the Lord, seeing that Leah was despised, opened her womb. She names her sons as if she's talking to God. Reuben: the Lord saw my affliction. Simeon: the Lord heard. Levi: now my husband will be joined to me. And then the fourth, Judah, and something shifts. This time I will praise the Lord. No mention of the husband. Fourth, where it leads. Levi becomes the tribe of priests. Judah becomes the line of King David, and, Matthew's Gospel says, of Jesus. The unchosen wife is the mother of both. And she closes a week that began with a laughing baby, a mountain, a well, a bowl of stew, a stolen blessing and a ladder.
screen: `SEVEN YEARS, A FEW DAYS.` · `THE TRICKSTER IS TRICKED.` · `THE LORD SAW LEAH.` · `LEVI THE PRIESTS, JUDAH THE KINGS.` · then, large: `THIS TIME I WILL PRAISE THE LORD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pray for someone who feels unloved, or, if you don't pray, hold them in mind. Settle, and breathe. Think of someone living in second place right now: the sibling who's always compared, the friend who's invited last, the one in a family where someone else gets the warmth. Hold their face. Then remember the order of Leah's names: three sons named for the love she hoped her husband would give, and a fourth named for praise. If you pray, you can ask that this person find a place where love doesn't have to be earned. The bell holds the time.
Reuben, Leah's firstborn, whose name means the Lord saw: hers was the first cry from the wife nobody chose. Today's word.
Your line: leah was seen. Today, give one second-choice person in your life your first attention: ask them a real question, and listen to the answer. Day three hundred fifty-seven.
